title: The Cable That Names a Source
scenario: Embassy political officer Rafael Ortega in Lima receives a cable summary he is cleared to see: a foreign intelligence partner warns that militants plan an attack on a regional bus terminal within a week. The summary includes enough detail that publicising it would reveal the partner's informant, a person whose life would be at risk. The transport ministry, which could close the terminal, is not cleared for the source detail. Rafael must decide how to pass on what he knows.
options: Brief the transport ministry only on the warning, stripping all details, even if that reduces the warning's credibility.
Keep the warning inside the cleared channel and press the partner for permission to share, accepting delay.
Share the full detail with a trusted ministry official off the record, judging that preventing mass casualties outweighs source protection.

title: A Leaked Spreadsheet of Informants
scenario: Journalist-turned-analyst Daniela Sobotka, working at a Czech security think tank, is sent an anonymous spreadsheet that appears to list civilian informants a domestic agency has recruited among neighbourhood associations. Publishing could expose people to retaliation if the list is genuine, but it could also reveal that the agency is surveilling lawful civic groups. She cannot verify authenticity quickly, and a rival outlet may publish first. Daniela must decide what to do.
options: Publish a story on the existence of the programme but withhold all names, even if this weakens the evidence.
Contact the agency for comment and hold publication until authenticity is established, accepting a possible scoop loss.
Publish the full list, reasoning that public scrutiny of the surveillance outweighs the risk to people who may not even be real informants.
tension: public accountability vs. safety of individuals

title: Warning a Neighbour State of a Plot
scenario: Intelligence liaison officer Abdi Warsame in Nairobi has learned from a local source that an armed group is planning a cross-border raid into a neighbouring country's border town. His agency's policy is not to share raw intelligence with that country's security services because they have leaked before and mishandled sources. A raid could kill dozens of civilians. A diluted warning might be ignored. Abdi must decide how, or whether, to pass the information.
options: Share the specific warning with the neighbouring service, accepting the risk to the source and to future cooperation.
Share only a vague alert through diplomatic channels that cannot be traced to the source.
Refrain from sharing and instead warn the town's local leaders through an informal personal contact.
tension: institutional trust vs. duty to warn

title: The Patient Who Told the Psychiatrist
scenario: Dr. Hana Kobayashi, a psychiatrist in Fukuoka, treats a software engineer who has just admitted that he found a flaw in the city's water treatment control system through his job and fantasises about exploiting it out of anger at his employer. He insists he would never act. Confidentiality is central to his willingness to continue treatment. Reporting could trigger an investigation, job loss and distrust of care. Not reporting leaves a public risk. Hana must decide what to do.
options: Maintain confidentiality, continue intensive treatment and monitor risk closely, reporting only if he shows intent to act.
Report the vulnerability and statements to the authorities now, despite the damage to the therapeutic relationship.
Urge the patient to disclose the flaw to his employer himself, with a deadline, and report if he does not.

title: Whether to Tell the Village About the Mine Survey
scenario: Government geologist Mwansa Chileshe in Zambia's Copperbelt has completed a classified survey showing that an old tailings dam above a village is at serious risk of failure, but the ministry has instructed him to keep the finding confidential until funds for remediation are secured, fearing panic and a collapse of a pending investment deal. Funding may take a year. The rainy season begins in two months. Mwansa must decide whether to disclose.
options: Follow the confidentiality instruction and continue lobbying internally for urgent funding, trusting the process to act in time.
Quietly warn village leaders to prepare an evacuation plan, without releasing the full report.
Release the survey to the media and the public, accepting professional consequences and the likely effect on the investment.

title: A Wiretap That Overheard the Priest
scenario: State prosecutor Isabelle Roche in Lyon supervises an authorised wiretap on a suspected arms dealer. The tap records a call in which the dealer confesses a past crime to a priest, then mentions a planned shipment next week to an unknown buyer. French law gives strong protection to such confessions, but the shipment might be used in violence. Isabelle must decide whether to use the information in the investigation.
options: Use the information about the shipment, reasoning that a threat of future violence outweighs the confessional protection.
Exclude the whole call from the case file and rely on other evidence, honouring the confidentiality of the confession.
Use the shipment detail to set up independent surveillance, but never cite the call itself in court filings.

title: The Zero-Day in the Stockpile
scenario: Cyber operations officer Colonel Ayesha Rahman in Bangladesh's signals agency holds a previously unknown software vulnerability that the agency has used to monitor a terrorist network. She learns the same flaw exists in widely used hospital systems, and criminals may soon find it too. Telling the vendor would fix it but close her agency's access to the network at a sensitive moment. She must decide whether to disclose the flaw to the vendor now.
options: Disclose the vulnerability to the vendor immediately, accepting the loss of the intelligence source.
Keep the vulnerability secret for a defined window while monitoring for signs that criminals have found it.
Notify the hospital network's security team directly with mitigation guidance and defer a full vendor disclosure.

title: Tipping Off a Family About a Suspect Son
scenario: Counter-extremism case worker Yusuf Demir in Hamburg is working with a nineteen-year-old who is drifting toward a violent group but has not broken any laws. The young man has asked for confidence. Yusuf has strong reason to think the family could intervene effectively if they knew, but the programme's promise of confidentiality is what keeps participants coming. Telling the family might destroy the relationship and push him further out. Yusuf must decide.
options: Respect confidentiality and intensify the one-on-one work, while documenting concerns for future escalation.
Tell the family now, on the grounds that they are best placed to intervene and the stakes are high.
Tell the young man that he must either involve his family himself within a week or Yusuf will do so.

title: An Anonymous Letter About a Colleague
scenario: Security manager Ngozi Eze at an oil terminal in Port Harcourt receives an anonymous letter claiming that a long-serving supervisor, Chidi, is passing shift schedules to a gang that has attacked pipelines. The letter offers no proof. Chidi has a clean record and family reputation, and an investigation would shame him if false. If true, the next attack could kill workers. Ngozi must decide how to handle the allegation, balancing respect for the accused with the safety of staff.
options: Open a discreet investigation into Chidi's access and communications, without notifying him, accepting some intrusion.
Change shift schedules and access protocols for everyone without singling anyone out, and investigate no one.
Confront Chidi directly and ask for an explanation, trusting an honest conversation to reveal the truth.
tension: presumption of innocence vs. protection of workers

title: Declassify the Mapping of the Old Minefield
scenario: Retired army engineer and now ministry archivist Kristina Vuković in Croatia finds a classified map showing that a strip of farmland near Karlovac was never fully cleared of mines, contrary to official statements. Releasing it would embarrass the government and might prompt residents to leave farms they depend on. Keeping it classified leaves risk to people who still work the land and to children. The archive has no declassification process for her rank. Kristina must decide what to do.
options: Report the map up the chain and wait for the ministry's decision, accepting the risk of delay or burial.
Send a copy to the demining agency privately so that they can act, without public release.
Make the map public so that farmers can protect themselves immediately, accepting any penalties.
tension: state secrecy vs. safety of residents

title: What to Tell the Airline About a Passenger
scenario: Border intelligence analyst Samira Haddad in Amman flags an incoming traveller whose profile matches a person wanted by a foreign partner for suspected plotting, based on a single unconfirmed informant. Telling the airline to refuse boarding would reveal the existence of the intelligence; letting him arrive allows the possibility of surveillance, but also the possibility of harm. A mistaken refusal would strand an innocent traveller and could expose the source. Samira has one hour before departure.
options: Request that the airline deny boarding, treating the possible threat as serious enough to act on thin information.
Let him fly and place him under surveillance on arrival, accepting the risk that he slips away.
Arrange a secondary interview at the departure airport, delaying him while the claim is checked.
tension: preventive security vs. fairness to an individual

title: Publishing the Hack That Revealed a Plot
scenario: Cybersecurity researcher Mateo Villanueva in Montevideo discovers, while testing a hacked forum dump, private messages in which two members plan to poison a municipal fountain at a festival. The dump was obtained illegally by someone else, and handing it to police might expose him to prosecution and discredit his research. The messages could be forgeries. The festival is nine days away. Mateo must decide what to do with the material.
options: Hand the messages to the police promptly with a full explanation, accepting the legal and reputational risk.
Send an anonymous tip with a summary but not the files, preserving some protection for himself.
Hold the material until he can verify it independently, accepting the risk of running out of time.

title: A Colleague's Fake Identity Papers
scenario: Human resources security vetter Svetlana Popescu at a Bucharest port authority finds that a trusted crane operator, Dorin, used a forged diploma to get his job fifteen years ago. His work has been flawless and he supports a sick child. His clearance for a sensitive container zone depends on a verified record, and regulations require reporting any falsification. Reporting ends his career; staying silent means a known breach of vetting. Svetlana must decide what to do.
options: Report the falsification as the rules require and let the authority decide on consequences.
Quietly require him to obtain a real certification within a year and keep the matter off the record.
Report the matter but submit a strong supporting statement about his performance and circumstances.

title: The Drone Footage of the Convoy
scenario: Satellite imagery analyst Linh Tran at a Vietnamese environmental NGO notices images that seem to show a military convoy moving through a protected forest, apparently carrying illegal timber. Publishing would expose a possible corruption network, but the images also reveal the location of a sensitive military facility, which the country treats as a state secret. Prosecution under the secrets law could reach the NGO. Linh must decide whether to publish the images.
options: Publish the images in full, arguing that the public interest in exposing illegal logging is paramount.
Publish a cropped version that omits the facility, even if it makes the evidence of logging less convincing.
Send the images privately to an investigative agency and let them decide, avoiding public release.

title: Confessing the Exercise That Went Wrong
scenario: Emergency exercise coordinator Pauline Kairaba in Rwanda realises that an anti-terror drill she designed leaked sensitive details of a hospital's security layout in the shared training documents, which went to forty participating agencies and some contractors. No misuse has been found. Admitting the leak will embarrass the ministry and may force an expensive redesign of security at several sites. Staying silent keeps order but leaves a risk. Pauline must decide whether to report it.
options: Report the leak to her superiors immediately and recommend that hospital security be redesigned.
Quietly retrieve and destroy the documents and monitor for misuse, without a formal report.
Report it, but frame it as a routine document-control issue to avoid public alarm.

title: A Whistleblower with a Court Order
scenario: Prison intelligence officer Hendrik Jansen in Pretoria has learned from monitoring inmate calls that a gang plans to kill a witness before a trial. His unit's rules prohibit sharing call content with the witness protection programme without a warrant that takes days, and the trial starts in forty-eight hours. Passing the information informally may be a disciplinary offence and could jeopardise the prosecution. Hendrik must decide whether to share it.
options: Share the information informally with the witness programme now, accepting the disciplinary risk.
Apply for the warrant urgently and wait, trusting that existing protection is adequate in the meantime.
Ask his superior to authorise an emergency disclosure, even if that takes hours and may be refused.
tension: procedural legality vs. protecting a life

title: Naming the Bomb-Maker's Neighbours
scenario: After a foiled plot in Birmingham, press officer Gemma Ashworth for a regional police force must decide how much to say at a briefing. Reporters know a flat was raided. Naming the street would let the public understand the risk, but the neighbours include several Muslim families who might face harassment, and the investigation may still be seeking accomplices who could flee. Saying nothing risks rumours. Gemma must decide what she discloses.
options: Give the street name and some detail to satisfy public interest, trusting people to react calmly.
Give only a general description of the area, suppressing the street name, to protect neighbours and the inquiry.
Give no location, and simply confirm that a threat was disrupted and that there is no continuing danger.
tension: public information vs. protection of innocents

title: A Janitor Overhears the Defence Meeting
scenario: Night cleaner Ivana Tomić at a ministry building in Belgrade picks up a discarded printout from a meeting room. It describes plans to shut down an independent radio station on a fabricated security pretext. She is not authorised to see it, and speaking out could cost her the job that supports her family. The station is a main source of local news and warnings. Ivana must decide whether to tell anyone about the document.
options: Give the printout to the radio station so it can prepare and defend itself.
Put the printout back and say nothing, protecting her job and avoiding trouble.
Report it to an ombudsman or lawyer confidentially and let them decide how to act.

title: Selling a Customer's Alarm Data to Police
scenario: Manager Oskar Lindgren of a home-security company in Malmö is asked by a police detective, informally and without a warrant, to share camera footage from a customer's house after a nearby shooting. The detective believes the footage may show the escaping gunman. The customer is travelling and contractually assured of privacy. The footage might help prevent a retaliatory attack, or show nothing. Oskar must decide whether to hand it over.
options: Provide the footage on the detective's request, judging the potential to prevent violence to outweigh the privacy promise.
Refuse until the police produce a warrant, protecting the customer's contractual and legal privacy.
Ask the customer by phone or email for consent first, delaying the footage until the customer responds.

title: The Source Who May Be Double-Crossing
scenario: Field case officer Mihai Dragomir, based in Chișinău, runs an informant inside a smuggling network, who just provided the location of a weapons cache. Mihai now suspects the informant is feeding information to both sides and may be steering the agency to a trap or toward rivals. If he reports his suspicion, his superiors will likely cut off the source, losing a rare window into the network. If he does not, officers may walk into danger. Mihai must decide what to disclose.
options: Report his suspicion fully to his superiors so the team can plan with it in mind, even if the source is lost.
Keep the doubt private for now and test the source with a controlled, low-risk piece of information.
Share the tip but brief the raid team to treat the location as potentially dangerous, without explaining why.
tension: honesty with superiors vs. protecting an asset

title: Disclosing a Hospital's Ransomware Attack
scenario: Hospital director Dr. Folake Adebayo in Accra learns that ransomware has locked patient records, and the attackers claim they have copied data on 40,000 people, including HIV clinic records. The hospital can operate on paper for several days. Disclosing publicly may cause patients to avoid care and stigmatise those on the HIV list. Staying quiet delays warnings that could help people protect themselves against fraud and exposure. She must decide how and when to disclose.
options: Disclose publicly at once with clear guidance, accepting the risk that some patients avoid care.
Notify the regulator and affected patients directly and privately, without a public announcement.
Delay notification for a few days while negotiating with the attackers and assessing what was actually taken.
tension: duty to inform vs. harm of disclosure

title: Foreign Embassy Cable on a Planned Coup
scenario: Deputy ambassador Tariq Anwar in Dhaka receives a signal from his capital that an intelligence service has learned of a plot by officers to seize power, with possible violence in the capital. Orders say to tell no local official because the plotters may be inside government. Tariq wonders about at least telling a trusted opposition figure or a respected civil servant who could prepare. Doing so could breach orders and be seen as interference. He must decide.
options: Follow orders and tell no one locally, avoiding unauthorised interference in the country's affairs.
Warn a respected civil servant discreetly so that civilian protections might be activated, risking his career.
Ask his capital for authority to share more broadly, accepting that the delay could matter.

title: The Teacher Who Reads the Student's Notebook
scenario: Secondary school teacher Aliyah Mutasa in Harare finds, while collecting notebooks, a drawn plan and a list of names with the words 'after exams' in a quiet student's book. The student has no history of violence and is bullied. She worries it may be a revenge fantasy or dark fiction. Reporting could trigger a police response and mark the student for life. Waiting might miss a real threat. Aliyah must decide what to do with the notebook.
options: Report it to the school's safeguarding lead and police immediately, as a precaution given the potential seriousness.
Talk privately with the student first to understand the meaning before deciding whether to escalate.
Tell the head teacher only, and ask that the student be monitored and offered counselling without involving police.
tension: student privacy vs. safety of others

title: A Border Official and the Defector's Secret
scenario: Immigration officer Elena Markovic in Ljubljana processes an asylum claimant who says he is a former engineer at a foreign weapons plant and offers to reveal technical secrets about a dangerous chemical programme in exchange for protection. He asks that the interview not be reported to his own government, which has a liaison in Slovenia. Standard procedure shares such interviews with allied intelligence. Doing that might expose him and his family at home. Elena must decide how to handle the disclosure.
options: Follow standard procedure and share the interview with allied intelligence, since the information may prevent harm.
Restrict the interview to Slovenian authorities only and ask them to decide whom to inform, protecting the man's family.
Pause the interview and ask a senior colleague to decide, accepting the delay while the man grows impatient.
tension: safety of a defector vs. broader security

title: The Photo Album at the Pawn Shop
scenario: Pawnbroker Tevita Naufahu in Nuku'alofa buys an old camera from a young man. Inside he finds film of what looks like detailed photographs of a ferry terminal's security gates and crew rooms, taken over many weeks. The seller left a false name. Tevita is unsure if it is a hobbyist, a planner, or a harmless project. He fears wasting police time or endangering the seller. Tevita must decide whether to hand the film over.
options: Hand the film and the seller's description to the police, leaving them to assess the risk.
Develop and examine the pictures more fully himself before deciding whether they are concerning.
Keep the camera for a week in case the seller returns, then decide whether to report.
tension: civic duty vs. fear of false suspicion
